351.quote_or_event: “But they do not cross the Flood of Life, who, ignoring the true relation of things, and not versed in the true Law, hold the above heretical opinions.” … “They do not put an end to birth, who, &c.”
351.explanation: After surveying views it considers false, the Sūtrakṛtāṅga concludes that anyone who misreads the true nature of things stays in the flood of saṃsāra and cannot end birth. In Jain terms, wrong view (mithyātva) heads the causes of bondage.
351.tie_back: The Kural traces inglorious birth to the delusion that takes the unreal for the real. The Jain text likewise ties the failure to end birth to ignorance of 'the true relation of things'.
351.source: Sūtrakṛtāṅga I.1.1.20 and 23 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895, p. 239)
351._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com. The causal link from misperception to continued birth matches well, though the passage is aimed at rival schools rather than offering a general account of delusion.

352.quote_or_event: “By the teaching of true knowledge, by the avoidance of ignorance and delusion, and by the destruction of love and hatred, one arrives at final deliverance which is nothing but bliss.”
352.explanation: Mahāvīra's sermon opens by naming the path: true knowledge, the removal of ignorance and delusion, and the end of passion lead to a liberation that is pure bliss.
352.tie_back: Valluvar promises that when delusion departs and stainless vision arises, darkness lifts and bliss follows. The Jain verse makes the same sequence explicit: delusion avoided, knowledge gained, 'final deliverance which is nothing but bliss'.
352.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 32.2 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895, p. 184)
352._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com. A close match of delusion removed, knowledge and bliss, though the light-and-darkness imagery is absent.

353.quote_or_event: “(The excellence of faith depends on the following) eight points: 1. that one has no doubts (about the truth of the tenets); 2. that one has no preference (for heterodox tenets); 3. that one does not doubt its saving qualities; 4. that one is not shaken in the right belief …”
353.explanation: In Jain teaching, freedom from doubt (niḥśaṅkita) is the first limb of right faith (samyag-darśana), the starting point of the path to liberation.
353.tie_back: Valluvar says that heaven is nearer than earth for those who have passed beyond doubt into clarity. Jainism likewise puts freedom from doubt first among the marks of the right faith that opens the road to liberation.
353.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 28.31 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895, pp. 156-157)
353._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com, with an ellipsis marking the omitted list. Doubt-free certainty matches aiyam neengi, but there is no equivalent of the Kural's 'heaven is nearer than earth' image.

354.quote_or_event: “Without (right) faith there is no (right) knowledge, without (right) knowledge there is no virtuous conduct, without virtues there is no deliverance, and without deliverance there is no perfection.”
354.explanation: The Uttarādhyayana sets out a strict chain: every later attainment depends on right faith and right knowledge, and nothing else can stand in for them.
354.tie_back: The Kural says that even complete mastery of the five senses brings no benefit without knowledge of the real. The Jain chain likewise makes all discipline and virtue fruitless without right knowledge of reality.
354.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 28.30 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895, p. 156)
354._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com. The principle that discipline is useless without true knowledge matches, but the verse does not mention the five senses or sensory knowledge specifically.

355.quote_or_event: “He who understands the true nature of all substances by means of all proofs (pramâṇa) and nayas, believes by a complete course of study.”
355.explanation: Jain epistemology examines every object through valid means of knowledge (pramāṇa) and partial standpoints (naya). No single appearance or angle is taken for the whole truth of a thing.
355.tie_back: Valluvar defines wisdom as seeing the true reality in each thing, however it appears. The Jain method of pramāṇa and naya, the basis of anekāntavāda, is a disciplined way of getting past appearances to a thing's true nature.
355.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 28.24 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895, p. 155)
355._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com. The ideal of grasping the true nature of every substance is a strong fit. The Jain verse frames it as one route to right faith rather than as a definition of wisdom.

356.quote_or_event: “Then he knows and sees all things, he is free from delusion and hindrances, his Âsravas have gone, and he is proficient in meditation and concentration of thoughts, and being pure he will arrive at beatitude when his life is spent.”
356.explanation: The dispassionate sage reaches omniscience (kevala-jñāna) while still alive, knowing and seeing all things. At the end of that life he passes into liberation, from which, in Jain teaching, a soul never returns.
356.tie_back: Valluvar's learned ones who have 'seen' the truth 'here' and take the path of no return match the Jain kevalin, who knows and sees in this very life and then reaches final release when his life ends.
356.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 32.109 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895, pp. 191-192)
356._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com. Knowing and seeing in this life, followed by release, matches closely. 'No return' is standard Jain doctrine about siddhas but is not stated in this verse.

357.quote_or_event: “1. jîva, Soul; 2. ajîva, the inanimate things; 3. bandha, the binding of the soul by Karman; 4. puṇya, merit; 5. pâpa, demerit; 6. âsrava … 7. saṃvara … 8. the annihilation of Karman; 9. final deliverance: these are the nine truths (or categories). He who verily believes the true teaching of the (above nine) fundamental truths, possesses righteousness.”
357.explanation: For Jainism, 'that which is' is spelled out as the nine tattvas, and firm conviction in them is the right view with which the path to the end of rebirth begins.
357.tie_back: Valluvar says that once the mind has examined and firmly grasped That Which Is, no further birth need be feared. The Jain counterpart is firm conviction in the real categories (tattvārtha), which is where the soteriological path starts.
357.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 28.14-15 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895, p. 154)
357._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com; Jacobi's g-spellings are rendered as j, and ellipses mark omitted glosses. The Jain 'reals' are a plural set of categories rather than a single Being, so the fit is thematic.

358.quote_or_event: “Love and hatred are caused by Karman, and they say that Karman has its origin in delusion; Karman is the root of birth and death, and birth and death they call misery.”
358.explanation: The Uttarādhyayana traces birth and death to karma and karma to delusion, and then calls birth and death themselves misery.
358.tie_back: Valluvar names 'the folly called birth'. The Jain verse also roots birth in delusion and treats birth as the very affliction that true insight removes.
358.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 32.7 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895, p. 185)
358._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com. The equation of birth with misery rooted in delusion is very close. The verse does not name the positive counterpart, the Kural's 'perfect Truth called excellence'.

359.quote_or_event: “Thus the objects of the senses and of the mind cause pain to passionate men, but they never in the least cause any pain to the dispassionate.”
359.explanation: After surveying all six sense-fields, the sermon concludes that pain can attach only where passion gives it something to hold. The dispassionate person offers no foothold.
359.tie_back: The Kural's wordplay on saar- (clinging) says that afflictions which would cling will not cling to one whose attachments have perished. The Jain verse states the same: objects that hurt the passionate cannot touch the dispassionate.
359.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 32.100 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895, p. 190)
359._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com. This matches the second half of the couplet well, but Jainism has no counterpart to the 'true Support of all things' that commentators read in the first saarbu.

360.quote_or_event: “I shall explain in due order the means which must be adopted by him who wants to thoroughly uproot love, hatred, and delusion.” … “He will get rid of all misery which always afflicts mankind; recovered from the long illness, as it were, and glorious, he becomes infinitely happy, and obtains the (final) aim.”
360.explanation: Mahāvīra's sermon sets out to uproot completely the triad of rāga, dveṣa and moha (love, hatred and delusion). It ends with the liberated sage cured of all misery 'as from a long illness'.
360.tie_back: Valluvar's triad of desire, anger and delusion, destroyed so completely that even their names are gone, and the suffering (noi, 'disease') ending with it, corresponds almost term for term to the Jain uprooting of love, hatred and delusion and the cure of the 'long illness'.
360.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 32.9 and 32.110 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895, pp. 185, 192)
360._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com. The triad and the disease metaphor both match closely. The Buddhist slot uses the parallel 'three poisons', but this is a distinct Jain canonical source.
